notes: 1 Jan 1970: BNP government of Chief Leabua Jonathan campaigning for the general election of 27 Jan 1970 (no coalition; slot 2 holds the small liberal UDP). BCP moved from MD slot 5 to slot 3 so the main opposition (c. 40% of the vote) starts with popularity. MFP moved from MD slot 0 to slot 14 (royalist non-aligned conservatives, has popularity). Slot 22 uses the Police Mobile Unit, as Lesotho has no army in 1970. Slot 23 is the royal house of King Moshoeshoe II.

0.name: Thebe ea Leabua
0.text:
Thebe ea Leabua, 'Leabua's Shield', is the hard core of ministers, loyal chiefs and police officers around Prime Minister Chief Leabua Jonathan who regard open competition with the Congress camp as a danger to the state. As Lesotho heads into the general election of 27 January 1970, they argue in private that power must not be surrendered whatever the ballot boxes say.

The group wants a strong executive, curbs on the king and the opposition, and close cooperation with Pretoria, London and the West against what it calls Congress communism. Its strength lies in the police, the chieftaincy network loyal to the BNP and the Catholic mission establishment.

1.name: Basotho National Party
1.text:
The Basotho National Party was founded in 1959 by Chief Leabua Jonathan with strong backing from the Roman Catholic mission and many chiefs. It narrowly won the pre-independence election of 1965 and has governed since independence in October 1966, with Jonathan as Prime Minister. On 1 January 1970 it is campaigning for the general election set for 27 January.

The BNP is conservative, anti-communist and pragmatic toward South Africa, on which landlocked Lesotho depends for jobs, trade and customs revenue. It courts Western aid, opposes Congress radicalism and draws its votes from Catholic villagers, women, chiefs and the farming districts of the lowlands.

2.name: United Democratic Party
2.text:
The United Democratic Party is a small opposition party founded in 1967 by Charles Mofeli. Without seats in parliament, it contests the general election of January 1970 as a third voice beside the two great camps of Lesotho politics.

The UDP presents itself as a liberal, constitutionalist alternative to the bitter rivalry between the BNP and the Basutoland Congress Party. It calls for clean administration, civil liberties, a non-partisan civil service and pragmatic relations with South Africa, and appeals mainly to clerks, teachers and traders in Maseru who are tired of the polarisation between chiefs and Congress militants.

3.name: Basutoland Congress Party
3.text:
The Basutoland Congress Party, founded in 1952 as the Basutoland African Congress, is the oldest nationalist party in the country and is led by Ntsu Mokhehle. It narrowly lost the 1965 election to the BNP and enters the general election of 27 January 1970 as the main opposition, confident of victory.

The BCP is Pan-Africanist and left-leaning, close to the Pan Africanist Congress of South Africa and hostile to apartheid. It demands land reform, curbs on chiefly privilege and economic independence from Pretoria, and its strength lies among migrant mineworkers, teachers, Protestant congregations and the educated youth of the towns.

4.name: Communist Party of Lesotho
4.text:
The Communist Party of Lesotho was founded in 1962 as the Communist Party of Basutoland, with John Motloheloa as its leading figure and close ties to the South African Communist Party. It is a small cadre organisation under constant pressure from the Jonathan government, which regards it as an instrument of Moscow.

The party follows a pro-Soviet Marxist-Leninist line, calls for nationalisation, land reform and a common front against apartheid, and tries to organise Basotho migrant workers in the South African mines. Its leverage lies in a handful of trade unionists and intellectuals and in its links to the international communist movement.

5.name: Bacha ba Roma
5.text:
Bacha ba Roma, 'the Youth of Roma', are the radical students and young lecturers of the University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland at its campus in Roma, the kingdom's only university. Stirred by the upheavals of 1968, the new Black Consciousness debates across the border and the liberation wars of Southern Africa, they form an unruly left beyond the Congress party.

They denounce the chiefs, the Catholic hierarchy and dependence on South Africa, call for a socialist Lesotho allied to the guerrilla movements, and pass around Fanon, Mao and Guevara. Their influence lies in student meetings, pamphlets and links to the Congress youth.

6.name: Bahlabani ba Thaba-Bosiu
6.text:
Bahlabani ba Thaba-Bosiu, 'the Warriors of Thaba-Bosiu', is a loose bloc of hardline traditionalists, initiation-school masters and village elders who invoke Moshoeshoe I's mountain fortress against everything they see as foreign. They distrust the mission churches, the Westminster constitution and the white-ruled republic that surrounds the kingdom.

They want Sesotho custom and chiefly authority restored over imported law, the lost lands west of the Caledon returned, and Lesotho freed from Western tutelage, even if that means seeking friends among the radical states of Africa and the East. Their leverage lies in village courts and the initiation lodges of the mountains.

7.name: Matla a Sechaba
7.text:
Matla a Sechaba, 'Power of the Nation', gathers Congress militants and returnees from Accra, Dar es Salaam and Cairo who have lost faith in elections organised by a BNP government. They admire the single-party states of independent Africa and believe Lesotho needs a disciplined vanguard rather than parliamentary bargaining.

The faction wants a one-party Congress state, a security service purged of British and South African influence, and arms and training from the Eastern bloc, China and Egypt. Its leverage lies in the hardline Congress youth branches and among exiles who have already passed through the training camps of Tanzania.

8.name: Anjuman-e-Haideri
8.text:
Anjuman-e-Haideri is a small Shia prayer and welfare circle among Indian-origin trading families in Maseru and the lowland towns, linked by kinship to Khoja communities in Natal and East Africa. With no Shia mosque in the country, it meets in private homes and keeps a low profile in a strongly Christian kingdom.

The circle favours an educated, reformist Shia identity, Muharram commemorations, religious schooling for children and loyal cooperation with the authorities. Politically it avoids partisanship and seeks trading licences and security for its members, while looking for religious guidance to the seminaries of Najaf and the jamaats of Mombasa and Dar es Salaam.

9.name: Majlis-e-Hussaini
9.text:
Majlis-e-Hussaini is a handful of young Shia men from trading families in Maseru and Mafeteng who have studied or travelled in Iraq and Pakistan and returned with a militant reading of the faith. They meet around cassette sermons and pamphlets from Najaf and Qom rather than with the cautious community elders.

They preach that only learned clergy can rightly guide Muslim life, reject accommodation with Christian and secular authority, and denounce the Shah of Iran as a Western puppet. Without numbers or legal standing, their leverage is limited to influence over a few households and contacts with radical clerical networks abroad.

10.name: Jamaat-ul-Muslimin
10.text:
Jamaat-ul-Muslimin is the modest Sunni congregation of Lesotho, made up of Indian-origin traders, Malawian migrants and a few Basotho converts who pray in a small mosque in Maseru. Its elders follow the ulama of Natal and the Deobandi seminaries of the subcontinent.

The community is loyal, quietist and anxious to avoid trouble with a Christian state: it asks only for freedom of worship, permission for Muslim schools and burial grounds, and protection of its members' shops. Its leverage lies in commerce and in charitable funds from Durban and the Gulf, which make it a small but steady presence in the capital.

11.name: Halqa-e-Khilafat
11.text:
Halqa-e-Khilafat is a tiny study circle of Muslim students and shop assistants in Maseru who have encountered the literature of Hizb ut-Tahrir and other pan-Islamic movements through contacts in Durban and London. It meets discreetly and has no public face.

Its members reject nation-states, parliaments and both superpowers as man-made idols and dream of a restored caliphate uniting all Muslims, from Africa to Asia. In Lesotho they can do little more than distribute leaflets and recruit among young migrants, but they regard themselves as the seed of a worldwide revival that will one day sweep away borders drawn by the colonial powers.

12.name: Halqat al-Ikhwan
12.text:
Halqat al-Ikhwan is a circle of educated young Muslims in Maseru, many of them students at Roma or teachers, who read Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb in English translation and correspond with Muslim youth groups in South Africa. They want a modern, organised Islam rather than the inward-looking piety of their elders.

The circle promotes Islamic education, social welfare and moral reform, accepts participation in elections and calls for justice for Palestine and for Africa's poor. Neutral between Washington and Moscow, it hopes to build a Muslim voice in public life, though its leverage remains confined to a few classrooms and community halls.

13.name: Marena a Maholo
13.text:
Marena a Maholo, 'the Principal Chiefs', are the twenty-two hereditary principal and ward chiefs who sit in the Senate and run local administration through their courts and the allocation of land. Most descend from Moshoeshoe I and his brothers and see themselves as the true backbone of the state, above party quarrels.

They favour authority, order and the chieftaincy's control of land, distrust both Congress populism and BNP attempts to subordinate chiefs to civil servants, and keep their distance from the great powers. Their leverage is the village itself: no field is allocated and no dispute settled without them.

14.name: Marematlou Freedom Party
14.text:
The Marematlou Freedom Party was formed in 1963 from the merger of the royalist Marema-Tlou Party and the Basutoland Freedom Party, and is the political vehicle of the supporters of King Moshoeshoe II. It won a handful of seats in 1965 and contests the general election of January 1970 as the third force.

The MFP wants a stronger constitutional role for the king, defends the chieftaincy and Sesotho tradition, and positions itself between the conservative BNP and the radical Congress. Its base lies among royalist chiefs, the king's partisans in the mountain districts and voters disillusioned with both large parties.

15.name: Lesotho National Development Corporation
15.text:
The Lesotho National Development Corporation was established by act of parliament in 1967 to attract investors, build industry and hold state shareholdings in a country with almost no manufacturing. Backed by the Jonathan government, it works with South African, British and other foreign firms and with the few Basotho businessmen able to join them.

Its circle of managers, contractors and partners wants tax holidays, cheap labour, tourism and diamond prospecting, stable relations with Pretoria and a business-friendly government. Its leverage lies in controlling the few new jobs, contracts and investment projects that Maseru can offer.

16.name: Bahoebi ba Basotho
16.text:
Bahoebi ba Basotho, 'the Basotho Traders', are African store-owners, wool and mohair buyers, transport operators and bakers who resent the grip of long-established white trading houses on Lesotho's commerce. Long held back by colonial licensing rules, they now want their share of independence.

They call for free licensing, lower duties, credit for African enterprise and an end to the monopolies of the old trading firms, while opposing state controls and socialist experiments alike. Their influence lies in the market towns, the wool sheds and the village stores that serve as bank, post office and meeting place for the rural population.

17.name: Mobu oa Rona
17.text:
Mobu oa Rona, 'Our Soil', is a network of agricultural officers, mission teachers and progressive farmers alarmed by the gullies that are washing Lesotho's thin topsoil into the Orange River. They build on decades of terracing and grazing-control schemes and on new aid-funded conservation projects in the lowlands.

They demand grazing limits in the Maloti highlands, tree planting, protection of wetlands and springs, and village committees to manage the land rather than chiefs allocating it at will. Their leverage lies in foreign development aid and in the growing fear that the kingdom is literally running out of soil.

18.name: Basebetsi ba Merafo
18.text:
Basebetsi ba Merafo, 'the Mineworkers', speaks for the tens of thousands of Basotho men who spend most of their working lives in the gold and coal mines of South Africa. Denied union rights across the border and absent from home for months at a time, they are the largest wage-earning group of the nation and a core Congress constituency.

The movement demands better contracts and deferred-pay schemes, protection from pass-law abuses, and jobs at home through industrialisation and land reform. It favours African socialism, non-alignment and solidarity with the liberation movements, and its leverage lies in the remittances that keep entire villages alive.

19.name: Pan Africanist Congress
19.text:
The Pan Africanist Congress, banned in South Africa since 1960, keeps underground cells among refugees, students and Basotho sympathisers in Lesotho. Its leader Potlako Leballo once directed the movement from Maseru, until the police raid on its office there in 1963 drove the leadership north to Dar es Salaam.

By 1970 the PAC leans toward Maoism and Chinese support, preaching armed struggle and an Africanist rejection of both white liberalism and Moscow-aligned communism. In Lesotho its leverage lies in close personal ties to the Basutoland Congress Party and the steady traffic of activists and recruits across the border.

20.name: Lefatše le Lahlehileng
20.text:
Lefatše le Lahlehileng, 'the Lost Land', is a populist movement of village orators, ex-servicemen and nationalist chiefs who never accepted the loss of the fertile Caledon lowlands to the Orange Free State in the nineteenth century. They keep the memory of the Conquered Territory alive at every public gathering.

They demand that the government press the land claim against South Africa, reserve trade and jobs for Basotho, and expel foreign traders and refugees they accuse of meddling in local politics. Their leverage lies in a grievance shared by almost every Mosotho, which any politician ignores at his peril.

21.name: Thupa ea Tšepe
21.text:
Thupa ea Tšepe, 'the Iron Rod', is a fringe of village toughs, young militants and disgruntled ex-policemen who believe Lesotho needs a single leader, a single party and the stick rather than the ballot. They break up rival meetings and settle scores with Congress supporters in the lowland districts.

They preach a cult of discipline and national unity under strong rule, despise both liberal democracy and communism, and would welcome emergency government with themselves as its enforcers. Their leverage lies in intimidation and in the protection some of them enjoy from local officials who find their services convenient.

22.name: Police Mobile Unit
22.text:
The Police Mobile Unit is the paramilitary wing of the Lesotho Mounted Police and the closest thing the kingdom has to an army. Formed for riot control and border security, it relies on British-trained officers and is loyal to Prime Minister Jonathan's government.

Its officers see themselves as the guardians of order against Congress unrest, cattle raiders and armed refugees crossing from South Africa, and they increasingly shape how the state responds to political crises. Its leverage lies in being the only armed body with vehicles, rifles and radios across the lowlands, able to decide the outcome of any confrontation in Maseru.

23.name: House of Moshoeshoe
23.text:
The House of Moshoeshoe, descended from the founder of the Basotho nation, reigns through King Moshoeshoe II, paramount chief since 1960 and king since independence in 1966. Educated at Oxford, the king has repeatedly clashed with Chief Leabua Jonathan over his powers and was briefly confined after the Thaba-Bosiu unrest of December 1966.

The royal house wants a monarchy that rules as well as reigns: a voice in foreign policy, control over the chieftaincy and a role as arbiter above the parties. Its leverage lies in the deep loyalty of the Basotho to the crown and in the support of the Marematlou Freedom Party.
